title: A difficult boss
hookLine: a Stoic, a monk and a Sufi would each counsel something different

lines: A STOIC, A MONK, A SUFI.
cards: An email arrives late on a Friday afternoon. The subject line is one word: urgent. Inside is an instruction that seems unfair, or unclear, or both, from the person who signs off on your work.

Three old teachers would read it very differently: a Stoic, who would read it from the sender's side; a monk, who would wait for the right moment to speak; and a Sufi poet, who would tell a story about a servant and a bitter fruit.
Each of them knew about taking orders. Today: Luqman.

teach.b: First, the Stoic. In his Handbook, Epictetus has advice for when someone treats you badly or speaks badly of you. Remember, he says, that they're doing what seems right to them; they can't follow what seems right to you.

If they've judged wrongly, they're the one deceived, and the one harmed. Start there, and you'll be mild toward them, saying each time: it seemed so to him. The point is to see the order from the giver's side.
Second, the monk. The Rule of Benedict has a chapter for a brother given orders that seem impossible.

He should first receive the command gently and obediently. If it truly looks beyond his strength, he should explain why to his superior, patiently, at a fitting time, without pride and without stubborn resistance.
If the superior still insists, the Rule says he should obey, trusting in God's help. Third, the Sufi. In Rumi's Masnavi there's a story about Luqman, a wise servant.
His master hands him a melon, and Luqman eats slice after slice as if it were sweet. When the master tastes it, it's so bitter it burns his mouth. Why didn't you say something?

Luqman answers, more or less: I've eaten so much sweetness from your hand, how could I complain of one bitter thing? Rumi tells it as a lesson in gratitude toward God, and some readers hear it about people too.
Fourth, the three don't agree, and that's useful: see the other side, speak up at the right moment, remember the sweet.
None of them is advice to put up with cruelty or harm. They're for the ordinary hard instruction that lands on a Friday afternoon.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns live under the Rule of Benedict, which sets out how to receive and question a superior's orders; Stoic readers return to Epictetus's Handbook on meeting ill treatment mildly; Rumi's Masnavi is read and recited in Sufi circles.

o: a Stoic teacher who wrote a handbook on duty
a monk's rule for obeying a hard command
a wise servant in Rumi who ate a bitter melon

games.q: who counsels what — tap the pairs.
p: when the monk should speak up

s: Epictetus says to answer someone who speaks ill of you with a sharper word
he says to remember they did what seemed right to them, and to be mild: it seemed so to him.
Benedict's Rule lets a monk explain why an order seems impossible
patiently, at a fitting time, without pride or stubborn resistance.
in Rumi's story, Luqman spits out the bitter melon
he eats it as if it were sweet, remembering the sweetness he'd received from his master's hand.

games.q: you're a monk in Benedict's monastery, and you've been given an order that seems impossible. what does the Rule say to do first?
o: refuse until the order is changed.
receive it gently, then explain patiently at a fitting time.
do it in silence and never say a word.
games.why: calm first, then an honest word at the right time, without pride. if the superior still insists, the Rule says to obey, trusting in God's help.

practice: Bring to mind one hard instruction and turn it around the way Epictetus would, saying silently: it seemed so to them. Like Benedict's monk, ask whether one honest sentence is worth saying, and when.
Then, like Luqman, remember one sweet thing from the same place, and if you pray, bring it to God in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Luqman. The wise servant in Rumi's Masnavi who ate the bitter melon without complaint, remembering all the sweetness that came before it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: calm under orders. Three counsels, and none of them asks you to bear cruelty. That's day nine hundred nineteen.

sources.ref: Masnavi, Book 2 (Luqman and the bitter melon)
